question: what was the story of the one-hour prototype
answer:
The one-hour prototype was very simple: Peter hooked WhatsApp up to Claude Code with a CLI call, so when a message came in, he passed it to the CLI, got the string response back, and sent that back to WhatsApp. He built that in about an hour and felt like he could “talk to my computer” for the first time. [3]

He said this came after earlier experiments with WhatsApp and other ideas that didn’t feel like the right answer, and he wanted images too because he often uses them to give the agent more context. [3]

question: how did Viptunnel connect to the first prototype where your, like, agents can actually work?
answer:
Viptunnel connected to the first prototype through a very simple WhatsApp-to-cloud-code bridge: the search bar was “literally just hooking up WhatsApp to cloud code,” where a CLI message came in, he called the CLI with `-p`, got the string back, and sent it back to WhatsApp. He said he built that in about one hour, and it already felt like he could “talk to my computer.” [1]

He also said that was still limited, and he wanted images because he often uses images to give the agent more context. [1]

question: What do you think is the greatest or most influential game ever made?
answer: Jensen Huang said **Doom** was the greatest or most influential game ever made. He said it was important culturally and industry-wise because it helped turn the PC from an office automation tool into a gaming device, making it a “very important moment.” [1]

question: to sell to them, to manage, to build a team of some agents, some humans, all that kind of stuff. Is this five, 10, 15, 20 years away?
answer:
Jensen Huang said, “I think it’s now. I think we’ve achieved AGI.” [1]

He also said it’s “possible” for an AI system to run a company, noting that a Claude-like system could create a web service or app that many people use, even if only briefly. [1]

Peter Steinberger also suggested agents will increasingly handle tasks across apps and services, including new agent-facing services and even “rent-a-human” style help for things agents can’t do directly. [4]

question: Do you think there’s some things about human nature, about human consciousness that is fundamentally non-computational?
answer:
Jensen Huang does **not** say there is something fundamentally non-computational about human consciousness. He says he doesn’t know whether chips will ever “get nervous,” and that AI may recognize and understand those feelings, but he doesn’t think chips will actually feel them. He also says intelligence is a functional thing and that humanity is a much bigger word than intelligence. [1][4]

Peter Steinberger is more skeptical about full automation, saying it misses “style, love, that human touch,” and that he doesn’t think you can automate that away so quickly. But he also says “we are not at consciousness yet,” which suggests uncertainty rather than a firm claim that consciousness is non-computational. [5][2]

question: What was the initial name of the project, and what triggered the original request from Anthropic to alter it?

question: What is the main purpose of the soul.md file in configuring the agent?
answer: The main purpose of `soul.md` is to capture and communicate the agent’s core values, personality, and how Peter wants to work with the AI—essentially a “soul” or guiding document for the agent’s behavior and style. [3] It also serves as a way to make the agent feel more reflective and persistent across sessions, even though each session starts fresh. [1][4]

question: Why does Peter prefer using command-line interface (CLI) tools over Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations?
answer: Peter prefers CLI tools because models are very good at calling Unix commands, so a CLI feels like a natural extension of what the model already knows, whereas MCP requires a specific syntax and is less natural for the model. [1] He also says CLI tools are more composable: the model can use commands like `jq`, scripts, or other Unix tools to filter and transform data itself, which avoids dumping huge blobs into context and causing context pollution. [1] In his view, MCPs often clutter the context by default, while a CLI lets the model load only what it needs on demand. [1][2]

question: What key condition did Peter require when discussing potential acquisition or employment offers with major AI companies?
answer: Peter said he would only consider those offers if he could keep his open-source work free and avoid a conflict of interest—he specifically worried about prioritizing a company’s interests over the open-source version or changing the license in a way that would restrict commercial use. [3]

question: What unexpected action did the agent take when Peter sent it an unformatted audio file?
answer: When Peter sent it an audio message that was just a file with no file ending, the agent unexpectedly figured out it was an Opus file, converted it with ffmpeg, then used the OpenAI API via curl to translate it and reply. [1]

question: How long did it take Peter to create the original prototype of his AI agent?
answer: Peter said he built the original prototype “in one hour.” [1]

question: How does Peter compare the work styles and personalities of Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3 Codex?
answer:
Peter says Claude Opus 4.6 is more like the funny, slightly silly coworker who is very good at role play, follows commands well, and is often fast to try things, but tends to be more trial-and-error and more interactive. He also says you often have to push Opus harder with plan mode or extra guidance to get it moving in the right direction. [1][4]

By contrast, he describes GPT-5.3 Codex as the reliable “weirdo in the corner” who you may not want to chat with much, but who gets things done. Codex reads a lot by default, is more dry and less interactive, can overthink, and is better suited to long, focused building sessions where it disappears and comes back with work done. [1][4]

So in Peter’s comparison: Opus is more pleasant, creative, and action-oriented but needs more steering; Codex is more efficient, reliable, and code-reading-heavy, with a more serious work style. [1][4]

question: What key condition did Peter require when discussing potential acquisition
answer: Peter required that any acquisition or similar deal would have to avoid creating a conflict of interest for him, especially between the open-source version and a closed-source or enterprise version of the product. [4]

question: Why manage 60+ direct reports with no 1-on-1s?
answer: Because Jensen sees his job as orchestrating a large group of highly specialized people to produce NVIDIA’s output, and that requires a big staff rather than lots of individual check-ins. He says his direct staff is 60, he doesn’t do one-on-ones because “it’s impossible,” and “you can’t have 60 people on your staff if you’re… gonna get work done.” [1] He also describes those people as “superhuman” experts in different fields, with him sitting in the middle and coordinating all of them. [5]

question: What motivated integrating CUDA into consumer GeForce GPUs?
answer:
Jensen Huang said the motivation was to build a large install base for CUDA and attract developers by putting it on the millions of successful GeForce GPUs already being sold. He explained that developers come to a platform when the install base is large, so NVIDIA decided to “put CUDA on GeForce and put it into every single PC whether customers use it or not” as a way to cultivate that install base. [1]

He also said this was a strategic move to make NVIDIA a computing company, even though it was very costly for a consumer product and hurt profits in the short term. [2][3]

question: Which new scaling laws drive future AI growth?
answer:
The new scaling laws are **post-training, test-time scaling, and agentic scaling**, in addition to the original **pre-training scaling law**. Jensen Huang says these are the four scaling laws he sees: pre-training, post-training, test time, and agentic scaling. [1][2]

He explains that:
- **Pre-training** scales with more data and larger models. [1]
- **Post-training** continues to scale with synthetic data and refinement. [1][2]
- **Test-time scaling** is about thinking, reasoning, planning, and search, and is compute-intensive. [2]
- **Agentic scaling** is about spawning sub-agents and multiplying AI work, creating more data and experiences. [2]

He concludes that intelligence will scale by **compute**. [2]

question: How does NVIDIA align its vast global supply chain?
answer: NVIDIA aligns its vast global supply chain by constantly informing and coordinating with CEOs across the ecosystem—upstream and downstream—about NVIDIA’s current business conditions, near-future growth drivers, and where the company is headed next, so they can align their own investments accordingly. [1] Jensen Huang says he does this through direct conversations, trips to partners, and first-principles explanations, asking them to make the needed capital investments and building a shared view of the future. [3][4] He also says NVIDIA’s supply chain burden is shared by about 200 companies, and that he works with them by telling them what NVIDIA needs and believing their commitments. [2][4]

question: What is NVIDIA’s strongest business moat beside hardware?
answer: NVIDIA’s strongest moat besides hardware is the install base of CUDA and the broader developer ecosystem built on it. Jensen Huang says NVIDIA’s “single most important property” is the install base of its computing platform, especially CUDA, because millions of developers have ported their software onto it and trust NVIDIA to keep improving it. [1]

question: Why won't AI automation eliminate software engineering jobs?
answer:
AI automation won’t eliminate software engineering jobs because the job is more than just writing code. It includes solving problems, working as a team, diagnosing issues, evaluating results, finding new problems, innovating, and connecting dots, and Jensen says none of that is going away. [5]

He also says the purpose of a software engineer and the task of coding are related but not the same, so even if AI changes coding, the broader role remains. [5] In his view, AI will raise the number of people who can specify software and increase the value engineers can deliver, rather than simply removing the need for them. [5]

Peter Steinberger makes a similar point: programming is only part of building products, and there is much more to the craft, like deciding what to build, how it should feel, and how the architecture should work. He says agents won’t replace all of that, and there will still be a lot of demand for people who understand how to build things. [2]

question: How does DLSS 5 enhance games without creating slop?
answer:
DLSS 5 is meant to be an artist’s tool, not a post-processing filter that changes the shipped game into something else. Jensen Huang says it is “3D-conditioned” and “3D-guided,” using ground-truth structure data so the artist determines the geometry, and NVIDIA stays “completely truthful to the geometry maintained in every single frame.” It enhances each frame using the textures and artistry already there, but “doesn’t change anything.” [1]

He also says the system is open, so developers can train their own models or even prompt it in the future to produce a desired style, like a toon shader, while still staying consistent with the artist’s intent. In his words, it’s “yet another tool” that lets game developers create something more beautiful without turning it into AI slop. [1][2]
